items.title: Myanmar earthquake reveals how fault history could help anticipate future slip
items.snippet: Earthquakes are full of unknowns—scientists can't accurately predict exactly when or where the next big earthquake will strike. But some characteristics of 'the next big one' can be anticipated from what we know about a fault before it breaks, thanks to supercomputer simulations combined with an ever-increasing wealth of observational data.

items.title: New workflow advances programmable chromosome editing in plants
items.snippet: A study published in Nature Protocols on Nov. 17 presents a detailed experimental workflow for programmable chromosome manipulation in plants. The platform was developed by a research group led by Gao Caixia at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

items.title: Sex in Britain has changed significantly, especially among young people
items.snippet: The sex lives of people in Britain have shifted markedly since 1990, and their sexual and reproductive health needs are substantial and varied, according to the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4). The first five papers from the survey—one of the largest studies of sexual behavior in the world—are published in The Lancet.

items.title: Microplastics in nearly 8 in 10 fish sampled off Oman's Sohar coast
items.snippet: Researchers at Sultan Qaboos University detected microplastics in the gills or digestive tracts of 95 of 120 fish sampled off Sohar in the Sea of Oman. Published in Scientific Reports, the study provides a baseline for tracking microplastic pollution in fish along this stretch of Oman's coast.

items.title: Carbon-rich soil near old oaks does not attract more earthworms, study finds
items.snippet: Solitary oaks in traditional Romanian wood pastures create islands of carbon-rich soil around their trunks.
